entities.name: Sulayman al-Arabi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sulayman ibn Yaqzan al-Kalbi al-Arabi, the Wāli of Barcelona and Girona in 777 CE, was a pivotal figure whose desperate alliance with Charlemagne inadvertently shaped the geopolitical landscape of the Iberian Peninsula. Facing the expanding power of the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba under Abd al-Rahman I, al-Arabi sought external intervention to preserve his semi-autonomous rule in the northeastern marches of al-Andalus. His actions underscore the complex, often fractured political realities within Muslim Iberia, where local rulers frequently prioritized regional autonomy over broader caliphal or emirate loyalties, even if it meant aligning with Christian monarchs.

In 777 CE, al-Arabi, along with other discontented Muslim leaders from Zaragoza and Huesca, traveled to Paderborn in Saxony to pledge fealty to Charlemagne and solicit military aid against Abd al-Rahman I. This unprecedented diplomatic overture led to the Frankish invasion of al-Andalus in 778 CE, a significant but ultimately disastrous campaign. Charlemagne's forces, expecting an easy conquest, marched as far as Zaragoza, but found the city's gates closed by Husayn al-Ansari, al-Arabi's own ally, who had since reneged on the agreement. During the retreat, al-Arabi was captured by Charlemagne's forces, who accused him of betraying the alliance, and was subsequently handed over to his Frankish allies. He was later freed by his sons, Matruh and Aysun, but was killed in 780 CE by al-Ansari, ostensibly for collaborating with the Franks.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sulayman al-Arabi's desperate alliance with Charlemagne, though personally disastrous, directly led to the Frankish invasion of al-Andalus and significantly contributed to the establishment of the Marca Hispanica, fundamentally altering the geopolitical balance in the northeastern Iberian Peninsula for centuries.
